1:
Ellicott marks the turn the chapter takes: having finished the furniture of the sanctuary, the account moves outward to what stood in the court, namely the brazen altar and the great laver. Henry makes the same division carry a contrast: the gold work, though the richest, had been ordered to lie most out of sight within the tabernacle itself, while what is now described stands open to the view of all, and both pieces are of brass. Calvin observes what is easy to miss in a chapter that repeats an earlier one, that the purport here is the same as before with the order of some parts transposed, though not a word is changed. Clarke sets out the whole chapter's contents at its head: the altar first, then the laver and its foot from the mirrors, the court with its pillars and hangings, the work finished by Bezaleel and Aholiab with their assistants, and last the reckoning of the gold, the silver and the brass. Gill explains why the making is ascribed to Bezaleel when the work was plainly not done by one pair of hands, namely that he had the care and oversight of it and it was made by his direction.

Comment on the structure divides between what it was and what it did. Clarke refers the reader back to the original instructions for the thing and for the Hebrew terms of its horns, pots, shovels and basins, treating the present chapter as an execution of what was there commanded. Calvin gives the purpose such exactness served: it was wrought of the materials and in the form God had prescribed, so the people might bring their offerings for expiation and thanksgiving with surer confidence. Henry states its function more strongly: every sacrifice was offered there, and being itself hallowed for the purpose by divine appointment it hallowed the gift laid upon it in faith. From that he passes to the use he wants, that Christ was himself the altar to his own sacrifice of atonement and is so to all our sacrifices of acknowledgment, so that we must have an eye to him in offering them as God has in accepting them. Wesley repeats those two sentences almost exactly as they stand.
8:
Clarke insists first on the rendering, since the English is misleading. The Hebrew word means a reflector of any kind, and what is meant here must be highly polished metal, glass not yet being in use; and had glass been in use, looking-glasses could not have furnished a brazen laver, which makes the received translation absurd. He then gives the history of the thing: the earliest mirrors were the still fountain and the unruffled lake, then mica, which splits into leaves so thin that a plate with something black behind it reflects well and is used in Russian warships in place of window glass; artificial mirrors began in brass, passed to polished steel and, as luxury grew, to silver, though very early ones were of tin and copper mixed, the best of them made at Brundusium. Ellicott supplies the object itself, that brass here means bronze and that Egyptian mirrors were bronze plates, round or oval with a handle, and that Etruscan women used the like, often delicately chased.

Why the women are mentioned at all is answered the same way by two voices and pressed further by one. Wesley takes the notice as honour paid them, since they were eminent for devotion and attended the place of public worship more constantly than others. Ellicott says what the gift cost, that mirrors were among the most highly prized of their possessions and were offered voluntarily, and what was done with it, that Moses marked his approval by forming their offerings into the most honourable of all the brazen vessels and recording the fact to their credit. On what physically became of them Wesley gives two possibilities and prefers the second: either they were artfully joined together or melted down and cast anew, but more likely the laver was burnished so brightly that its sides still served as mirrors, so that priests coming to wash might see their faces and discover the spots they came to cleanse. Gill adds a point of accounting, that the laver was not made from the brass of the offering, out of which the altar, its grate and vessels, the sockets and the pins were made, since the laver is not named among them.

The court draws a reading that Henry states and Wesley repeats almost word for word. Its walls were hangings like the rest, and they represented the state of the church under the older covenant, a garden enclosed, the worshippers confined to a little compass; but the enclosure being of curtains only intimated that the confinement of the church to one nation was not to be perpetual, the whole dispensation being movable and mutable, to be taken down and folded up when the place of the tent should be enlarged and its cords lengthened to make room for the Gentile world. Henry carries it further than Wesley follows him. The church on earth is only the court of God's house, and those who tread these courts are passing through them to the holy place above; and the enclosing of a court before the tabernacle teaches a gradual approach, since the priests had to pass through the holy court before entering the holy house. Clarke and Gill both leave the court to their earlier notes on the passage where it was first commanded.
21:
Why an audited reckoning belongs in the record at all is answered differently by each. Calvin says the point is not the fabric or the architecture but the perpetual conservation of it, that Ithamar deposited the several parts with the Levites so they should know what they had in charge and nothing be lost; and he takes the counting itself as evidence that every man honestly discharged his duty and that none was drawn aside by covetousness so as to fall from his integrity. Henry describes the procedure, that Bezaleel and Aholiab brought in the account, Ithamar audited it and gave it to Moses, and that the young priest was thus trained up by lesser services and fitted for greater. Ellicott works on the opening phrase, reporting two renderings offered for it, these are the accounts and this is the reckoning, and correcting the following clause to a service of the Levites rendered by Ithamar's hand. Clarke states plainly that what precedes is a detail of everything the two workmen had been commanded to make. Ellicott also removes a mistranslation from the description of Aholiab, since the word rendered engraver means a worker in any material whatever and should be artificer.

On what the metals were worth the estimates diverge widely and the commentators say so. Ellicott reports three for the gold alone, running from nearly three hundred and twenty thousand pounds down to a hundred and seventy-five and then to a hundred and thirty-two thousand, and concludes that on any of them the amount was remarkable and showed both the liberal spirit of the people and a general sense that the occasion required lavish expenditure; he adds that there is no difficulty in supposing they had it, since they carried a great quantity of ornaments out of Egypt. Keil reaches a figure close to the lowest of these by his own reckoning. Henry and Wesley both give a round hundred and fifty thousand. Clarke declines to state any figure without first laying out the whole system of ancient reckoning, talents divided into minas and minas into drachms, and settling the value of the shekel, which he takes at three shillings where others make it less. Keil meanwhile extracts an arithmetical proof from the text itself: six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty men at half a shekel each yield a sum which, set against the hundred talents and the remainder, shows incidentally that a talent contained three thousand shekels.

The gold came in freely and the silver by assessment, and that contrast is what the expositors take away. Henry marks it plainly, that every man brought gold as he could and would while the silver was levied as a kind of poll-money. Wesley draws the public lesson, that since the one was raised by voluntary contribution and the other by tribute, either way may be taken for defraying public expenses provided nothing be done with partiality. Ellicott arrives at the same ground independently and puts it more sharply, calling it remarkable that compulsory payment toward the fabric of the sanctuary should be sanctioned at the very moment when the greatest stress was being laid on the acceptableness of voluntary gifts, and concluding that church rates, whatever be thought of their expediency, are defensible in principle from both Testaments. Clarke instead asks why so much wealth was required, and gives three reasons: to impress the people with the dignity of the divine majesty, to take out of their hands riches they had no use for in the wilderness and which might have bred the love that is the root of all evil, and to check pride by making them surrender even personal ornaments. Gill and Ellicott both explain the half-shekel from the root meaning to divide, and Gill weighs the brass in Paris pounds and supposes it came from the Arabian mountains.
